faq.q: Do we yawn because we need more oxygen?
faq.a: That is a popular idea, but experiments did not support it: people breathing extra oxygen or extra carbon dioxide yawned just as often.
It is one of the leading ideas. The big jaw stretch and deep breath may increase blood flow and bring cooler air and blood towards the brain. Some studies support it, but it is not settled.
asks: Tell me about the blood flow changes

faq.a: Seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can make you yawn. This contagious yawning is linked to social connection: it happens more between friends and family, but scientists are still studying why.
asks: Why do I yawn when someone else yawns?

faq.a: Yawns are common just after waking up, when getting sleepy, and when bored, moments when the brain is changing how alert it is.
asks: Why do we yawn when tired?

faq.a: Yes. Most vertebrates, including dogs, cats, birds and fish, yawn. Some, like dogs and chimpanzees, can even catch yawns.

facts: Human fetuses yawn in the womb from around 11 weeks of pregnancy.
Experiments in 1987 by Robert Provine found that breathing extra oxygen did not reduce yawning.
